questions.stem: The relationship between the internet and the web is that:
options: The web is a subset of the internet — hypertext documents and resources accessed through browsers
The internet is one of several services that run over the web
They are two names for the same global network
The web is the physical infrastructure; the internet is the software layer running on top of it
questions.explanation: The internet is the global network of connected devices; the web relies on that infrastructure but is only one service running over it, alongside email, FTP and VoIP. (B) and (D) are both the relationship stated backwards.

questions.stem: A data packet contains all of the following except:
options: The payload
Sender and receiver IP addresses
The complete route the packet will follow from source to destination
A sequence number used for reassembly
questions.explanation: A packet carries its destination, not its itinerary — each router decides the next hop independently, which is exactly why packets can arrive out of order. Packets also carry error-checking information. Smaller packets are faster and more reliable, since a loss costs only that packet.

questions.stem: Packets from a single request may arrive out of order because:
options: The browser requests the resources out of order to speed up rendering
The server transmits packets in whatever order it finishes generating them
Routers may forward packets along different routes, so they experience different delays
The receiving device processes packets as each one finishes error-checking, which varies with size
questions.explanation: This is exactly why each packet carries a sequence number — so the receiving device can reassemble them correctly regardless of arrival order.

questions.stem: DNS is best described as:
options: The system that assigns an IP address to a device when it joins a network
The protocol that establishes an encrypted connection to a named host
The system that translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses
The routing table that determines which path a packet takes to its destination
questions.explanation: "The phonebook of the internet", operating on port 53. (A) is DHCP — the sharpest trap, since both hand out addresses, but DHCP assigns them to devices while DNS looks them up by name.

questions.stem: The TCP three-way handshake is:
options: SYN → ACK → SYN-ACK
SYN-ACK → SYN → ACK
ACK → SYN → SYN-ACK
SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK
questions.explanation: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK — The client proposes, the server acknowledges and proposes in one message, the client acknowledges — confirming both sides are ready before any data is sent.

questions.stem: Place these in the correct order for loading a web page:
options: DNS lookup → HTTP request/response → TCP handshake → packet reassembly → rendering
TCP handshake → DNS lookup → HTTP request/response → packet reassembly → rendering
DNS lookup → TCP handshake → HTTP request/response → packet reassembly → rendering
DNS lookup → TCP handshake → packet reassembly → HTTP request/response → rendering
questions.explanation: Resolve the name to an address, establish the connection, exchange the request and response, reassemble the packets, then render. Every option contains the same five steps, so this cannot be answered by elimination.

questions.stem: IPv4 addresses are:
options: 32-bit, written as four decimal octets 0–255, giving roughly 4.3 billion addresses
32-bit, written as eight hexadecimal groups, giving roughly 4.3 billion addresses
128-bit, written as four decimal octets, giving roughly 340 undecillion addresses
64-bit, written as four hexadecimal groups
questions.explanation: (B) and (C) each pair one correct IPv4 property with one borrowed from IPv6 (128-bit, hexadecimal groups). The exhaustion of that ~4.3 billion address space is the reason IPv6 exists.

questions.stem: HTTPS operates on which port?
questions.explanation: 443 — HTTP is 80, SSH/SFTP 22, IMAP 143. Also worth knowing: FTP 21, SMTP 25, POP3 110, DNS 53.

questions.stem: Which protocol sends outgoing email?
options: POP3
SMTP
IMAP
SFTP
questions.explanation: SMTP — (port 25) — send-only. It reads the mail header for the receiver's address, queues the message, then removes it from the outgoing list once delivered. POP3 and IMAP only retrieve.

questions.stem: The key difference between POP3 and IMAP is:
options: POP3 operates on port 143 and IMAP on port 110
POP3 keeps mail synchronised on the server; IMAP downloads it and removes it to one device
POP3 retrieves mail only; IMAP both retrieves and sends it
POP3 downloads mail and removes it from the server to one device; IMAP keeps it synchronised on the server across devices
questions.explanation: POP3 = 110, IMAP = 143 — (A) has them swapped, and (B) has the behaviours swapped. IMAP also allows multiple users to access the same mailbox. Neither protocol sends, which rules out (C).

questions.stem: Well-known port numbers occupy which range?
questions.explanation: 0–1023 — (C) is the registered range and (D) the dynamic/private range — both are real, which is what makes them tempting.

questions.stem: SFTP differs from FTP because it:
options: Uses port 22 but can carry only text files, since binary data cannot be tunnelled over SSH
Wraps the FTP protocol in TLS on port 21, using port 20 for the data channel
Encrypts the file contents but still transmits the login credentials in the clear
Transfers files over an encrypted SSH stream on port 22, whereas FTP sends credentials and data in the clear on port 21
questions.explanation: (B) is the sharpest trap — it describes FTPS, a genuinely different protocol that adds TLS to FTP rather than tunnelling over SSH. Plain FTP transmitting credentials in the clear is a direct confidentiality failure on any shared network.

questions.stem: An HTTP 404 status code means:
options: Not Found
Forbidden
Bad Request
Internal Server Error
questions.explanation: Not Found — the server understood the request but has no such resource. (B) is 403 (the resource exists, you may not have it), (C) is 400 and (D) is 500. 200 is OK. Note that 4xx blames the client and 5xx blames the server.

questions.stem: GET should never be used for sensitive data because:
options: GET requests cannot be sent over HTTPS, so their parameters travel in plaintext
GET requests are unauthenticated, so the server cannot verify who sent them
GET is limited to 255 characters, so longer sensitive values are silently truncated
Parameters appear in the URL, which is bookmarkable, cacheable, and logged by proxies, browsers and servers
questions.explanation: (A) is a common misconception: over HTTPS the URL is encrypted in transit — the problem is everything that happens to it at either end. POST sends data in the request body and is used for submitting forms and creating or modifying records; GET should be safe and idempotent.

questions.stem: A router's role in packet delivery is to:
options: Forward packets between networks towards their destination IP address
Reassemble packets into the correct order using their sequence numbers
Translate the domain name in each request into an IP address
Verify each packet's checksum and request retransmission of any that fail
questions.explanation: Reassembly (B) happens at the destination device, name resolution (C) is DNS, and error recovery (D) is handled by TCP at the endpoints — routers forward, and that is deliberately all they do.

questions.topic: Big data, W3C and web architecture
questions.stem: The five Vs of big data are:
options: Volume, velocity, variety, validity, value
Volume, velocity, variety, veracity, value
Volume, velocity, variety, veracity, visualisation
Volume, velocity, variability, veracity, value
questions.explanation: Each distractor changes exactly one word, so this cannot be sight-read. Veracity is the one most often forgotten — the quality, accuracy, integrity and credibility of the data, i.e. how far it can be trusted.

questions.topic: Big data, W3C and web architecture
questions.stem: Veracity in big data refers to:
options: The rate at which new data arrives and must be processed
The range of formats and sources the data arrives in
The usefulness of the insight that can be extracted from the data
The quality, accuracy, integrity and credibility of the data
questions.explanation: The distractors are the other four Vs: (A) velocity, (C) value, (B) variety. Data may have missing pieces, be inaccurate, or simply fail to support any insight — all veracity problems.

questions.topic: Big data, W3C and web architecture
questions.stem: Big data pushes web architecture toward:
options: Vertical scaling — larger and more powerful single servers
Client-side processing, moving computation onto the user's device
Distributed systems, microservices and cloud computing, scaling horizontally
Edge caching, so that one monolithic server handles fewer requests
questions.explanation: (A) is the alternative that big data specifically outgrows — there is no single machine large enough. (D) is a real technique but addresses latency, not processing scale. Named frameworks: Hadoop and Apache Spark.

questions.topic: Big data, W3C and web architecture
questions.stem: Metadata in a streaming service is used to:
options: Store a compressed copy of the video for low-bandwidth clients
Categorise content, diagnose faults and personalise delivery without processing the full content
Record the encryption keys protecting each stream
Hold the viewer's playback position so a session can resume on another device
questions.explanation: Metadata is data about data — analysing it is far cheaper than analysing the video itself. (D) is real functionality but is session state, not metadata's defining purpose. The three types are structural (HTML tags), descriptive (file names, tags) and administrative (file permissions).

questions.topic: Big data, W3C and web architecture
questions.stem: Adaptive bitrate streaming works by:
options: Compressing the video once at upload into a single optimised file
Switching between pre-encoded quality levels in real time to match available bandwidth
Buffering the entire file on the client before playback begins
Permanently reducing the frame rate whenever the connection degrades
questions.explanation: The key word is pre-encoded — the service prepares several quality tiers in advance and the player switches between them mid-stream. (D) is the near-miss: it changes quality, but permanently and along the wrong axis. It is a big-data-driven decision, alongside CDN placement and recommendation systems.

questions.topic: Big data, W3C and web architecture
questions.stem: The W3C was founded in:
options: 1994 by Tim Berners-Lee
1989 by Tim Berners-Lee
1994 by the IETF
1989 by Vint Cerf
questions.explanation: 1994 by Tim Berners-Lee — 1989 is when he proposed the web at CERN — five years earlier — which is what makes (B) so tempting. The W3C develops open standards so the web remains interoperable and accessible.

questions.topic: Big data, W3C and web architecture
questions.stem: WCAG is produced by which W3C initiative?
options: The Machine-Readable Data Activity
The Internationalisation Activity
The Web Platform Incubator Community Group
The Web Accessibility Initiative (WAI)
questions.explanation: WAI — WCAG's four principles: content must be perceivable, operable, understandable and robust. ATAG and UAAG, from the same initiative, cover authoring tools and user agents respectively.

questions.topic: Big data, W3C and web architecture
questions.stem: Which W3C area covers Unicode, UTF-8 and bidirectional text?
options: Web security
Machine-readable data
Accessibility
Internationalisation
questions.explanation: Internationalisation — non-Latin scripts, right-to-left languages, and localising date formats, currencies and text direction. (C) is the closest trap: making content readable in another language is internationalisation; making it usable with assistive technology is accessibility.

questions.topic: Big data, W3C and web architecture
questions.stem: RDF, SPARQL, JSON-LD and Schema.org are W3C standards for:
options: Accessibility — describing page structure for assistive technology
Machine-readable data — representing and querying linked data
Internationalisation — encoding text in any script or writing direction
Web security — declaring which resources a page is permitted to load
questions.explanation: RDF represents information as a graph, SPARQL queries RDF, JSON-LD is a lightweight linked-data format, and Schema.org standardises structured data for search engines. (D) describes CSP, which is a real W3C security standard — just not this one.

questions.topic: Big data, W3C and web architecture
questions.stem: WebAuthn is a W3C standard for:
options: Encrypting cookies at rest inside the browser's storage
A response header declaring which sources a page may load scripts from
Passwordless, strong authentication using public key cryptography
Federating identity across sites by exchanging bearer tokens
questions.explanation: The device holds a private key and signs a challenge; the site holds only the public key, so there is no password database to steal. (B) is CSP and (D) is OAuth-style federation — both adjacent to WebAuthn in the W3C's web security work.

questions.stem: The three client-side technologies and their roles are:
options: HTML structure · CSS appearance · JavaScript interactivity
HTML structure · JavaScript appearance · CSS interactivity
HTML appearance · CSS structure · JavaScript interactivity
HTML content · CSS interactivity · JavaScript structure
questions.explanation: Every option contains all three technologies, so only the role mapping distinguishes them. Semantic HTML elements (nav, main, header) also carry meaning for screen readers, so structure is an accessibility concern as well.

questions.stem: Which of these is a back-end framework?
options: Flask
Bootstrap
Tailwind
React
questions.explanation: Flask — (Python). (D) is the sharpest trap — React is substantial and often called a "framework" in conversation, but it runs in the browser. Other back-end options: Django (Python), Express.js (Node.js), Ruby on Rails, Laravel (PHP). Bootstrap and Tailwind are CSS frameworks.

questions.stem: In Flask, the @app.route decorator:
options: Binds a model class to its corresponding table in the database schema
Registers a function to run before every incoming request is processed
Declares globally which HTTP methods the application will accept
Maps a URL path to the view function that handles requests for it
questions.explanation: (B) is @app.before_request and (A) is the ORM's job — both are real parts of a Flask application, just not this decorator. Elsewhere: request handles incoming HTTP requests, jsonify returns JSON responses, session manages session data, and the app's secret_key signs that session data.

questions.stem: The main structural difference between SQL and NoSQL databases is:
options: SQL uses a fixed schema and favours consistency; NoSQL uses a flexible schema and scales horizontally more easily
SQL allows each record its own fields; NoSQL enforces one fixed schema across a whole collection
SQL stores only structured data; NoSQL stores only unstructured data and cannot be queried
SQL runs on the server; NoSQL runs inside the client's browser
questions.explanation: (B) is the distinction exactly reversed. MongoDB and Firebase are NoSQL examples — records in the same collection may legitimately have different fields, which is the flexibility and the risk.

questions.stem: An ORM such as SQLAlchemy maps:
options: A template file to the data used to render it
URL paths to the view functions that handle them
Tables to classes, rows to objects, and columns to object attributes
A model class to the JSON structure returned by an API endpoint
questions.explanation: (B) is routing, (A) is the template engine, (D) is serialisation — all four are layers of the same back-end stack. Pros: simpler for OOP developers, less repetitive SQL, and it prevents SQL injection by parameterising queries. Cons: overhead on high-performance queries and difficulty with complex or legacy schemas.

questions.stem: A template engine such as Jinja2:
options: Removes unused rules from a stylesheet before deployment
Applies pending schema changes to the database
Converts an object into JSON for an API response
Generates HTML dynamically by combining a template with data
questions.explanation: It is what lets a single page template render for thousands of records without duplicating markup. (A) is PurgeCSS, (B) is a migration tool and (C) is a serialiser.

questions.stem: The correct back-end request flow is:
options: Browser → database → framework → web server → response
Browser → framework → web server → database → objects/libraries → response
Browser → web server → framework (routing, request parsing, business logic, response generation) → objects/libraries → database → response
Web server → browser → framework → database → response
questions.explanation: All four options contain the same components in different orders. Knowing the sequence is what lets you say where in the stack a control such as authentication or validation belongs.

questions.stem: A cookie differs from local storage because a cookie:
options: Is encrypted by the browser by default, whereas local storage is held in plaintext
Is sent to the server with every request, which makes it the usual carrier of a session ID
Persists with no expiry, whereas local storage is cleared when the tab is closed
Is readable only by server-side code, whereas local storage is readable only by JavaScript
questions.explanation: This automatic transmission is precisely why cookies need HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite attributes — and it is also what makes CSRF possible. (C) swaps the behaviours of local storage and session storage; (D) half-describes HttpOnly, which is opt-in rather than default.

questions.stem: Which dev tools tab shows which files loaded and how long each took?
options: Network
Performance
Application
Sources
questions.explanation: Network — (B) is the closest trap — Performance profiles what the page did over a timeline (scripting, layout, paint), whereas Network lists the individual requests. Application holds cookies and local/session storage; Sources debugs JavaScript.

questions.stem: A browser's rendering engine:
options: Compiles the server's template code into HTML before the response is sent
Executes JavaScript, leaving HTML and CSS to a separate layout process
Interprets HTML, CSS and JavaScript output to lay out and paint the page, and differs between browsers
Negotiates the TLS connection and verifies the server's certificate
questions.explanation: (B) describes the JavaScript engine (V8, SpiderMonkey), which is a distinct component that sits alongside the rendering engine (Blink, WebKit, Gecko). Vendor prefixes such as -webkit- exist precisely because engines implemented features at different times, which is why cross-browser testing matters.

questions.stem: In CSS, a class selector begins with . and an ID selector with #. The key rule about IDs is:
options: An ID may be applied to many elements, whereas a class identifies one unique element
An ID may be used only once per page, whereas a class may apply to many elements
An ID can be targeted only by CSS, whereas a class can also be targeted by JavaScript
An ID overrides an inline style, whereas a class does not
questions.explanation: (A) is the rule reversed. (D) is the tempting one for anyone who has just learned specificity — inline styles actually beat an ID selector, and only !important overrides them.

questions.stem: CSS specificity, from lowest to highest, is:
options: class → element → ID
ID → class → element
element → class → ID
element → ID → class
questions.explanation: element → class → ID — When several rules apply, the most specific wins — which is why over-using IDs makes a stylesheet hard to override and maintain.

questions.stem: The CSS box model, from inside out, is:
options: content → padding → border → margin
content → border → padding → margin
margin → border → padding → content
content → margin → border → padding
questions.explanation: Padding is inside the border; margin is the space outside it. (C) is the correct sequence read outside in — check which direction the stem asked for before answering.

questions.stem: Which method of applying CSS is recommended for a multi-page site?
options: A single external stylesheet linked from every page
An internal <style> block repeated in the head of each page
Inline style attributes on each element
An @import rule inside each page's internal style block
questions.explanation: External — One change updates every page, the file is cached across the whole site, and the markup stays clean. (D) is the near-miss: it does centralise the rules, but each @import blocks rendering while it resolves, so it is slower than a plain <link>.

questions.stem: @media (max-width: 768px) applies to:
options: Viewports up to and including 768px wide
Viewports of at least 768px wide
Any element whose parent container is narrower than 768px
WebKit-based browsers only, since the rule carries no vendor prefix
questions.explanation: max-width sets a ceiling, so the rule targets smaller screens — the mobile-first inversion of this is min-width, which is (B). (C) describes a container query, a different feature entirely. Responsive design combines media queries, relative units (rem, %) and the viewport meta tag.

questions.stem: The viewport meta tag <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0"> exists to:
options: Improve search ranking by declaring the page mobile-friendly
Instruct the browser to request smaller image assets on small screens
Register the service worker that a progressive web app requires
Set the layout viewport to the device's own width so a responsive stylesheet applies correctly
questions.explanation: Without it, mobile browsers assume a desktop-width viewport (typically 980px) and zoom out, which makes a perfectly good responsive stylesheet appear not to work at all.

questions.stem: Which of these is a CSS preprocessor rather than a framework?
options: PostCSS
Tailwind
Sass
PurgeCSS
questions.explanation: Sass — (with Less) — it adds variables, nesting and file splitting to a language that is compiled down to CSS. (A) is the sharpest trap: PostCSS transforms CSS after it is written (minifying, adding prefixes), which makes it a post-processor. PurgeCSS removes unused rules; Tailwind is a framework.

questions.stem: The trade-off of using a CSS framework such as Bootstrap is:
options: A smaller stylesheet than hand-written CSS, at the cost of losing responsive behaviour
Fast, consistent, tested responsive components, at the cost of a generic look and a large volume of unused CSS
Complete design freedom, at the cost of having to build your own grid system
Guaranteed accessibility compliance, at the cost of much longer build times
questions.explanation: The unused-CSS cost is exactly why PurgeCSS exists in the same toolchain. (D) is tempting because frameworks do ship accessible component markup — but that is a head start, not a guarantee.

questions.stem: The difference between a library and a framework is:
options: A framework is code you call; a library provides a structure that your code fits into
A library is code you call; a framework provides a structure that your code fits into
A library runs on the client; a framework runs on the server
A library is a single file; a framework is a collection of many files
questions.explanation: This is often put as inversion of control: you call a library, but a framework calls you. jQuery is a library; React and Bootstrap impose structure and conventions.

questions.stem: In Git, git add . performs which action?
options: Uploads the local commits to the remote repository
Records the staged changes as a permanent snapshot in the local history
Stages all changed files in the working directory into the staging area
Retrieves and merges the latest changes from the remote repository
questions.explanation: Stage — (B) is commit, (A) is push, (D) is pull — the four options are the four core commands in sequence. git commit -m "message" then creates the snapshot with a hash, timestamp, author and message; git log --oneline shows history, newest first.

questions.stem: A merge conflict occurs when:
options: Two branches have changed the same lines, so Git cannot decide automatically which to keep
Two developers push commits to the remote at the same moment
A branch has fallen so far behind main that Git refuses to merge it
A commit is made without a message, so Git cannot record what changed
questions.explanation: Note it is the same lines, not the same file — Git merges changes to different parts of a file without complaint. It is the practical argument for small, frequent commits and short-lived branches.

questions.stem: Branching in version control allows a developer to:
options: Rewrite the project's history to remove commits that are no longer wanted
Keep a compressed copy of the repository as it stood at a chosen point in time
Develop a feature in isolation from the main working version, then merge it back once tested
Work on a copy of the repository that is deliberately never synchronised with the remote
questions.explanation: (B) is a tag or an archive and (A) is a rebase — both real Git capabilities, neither is branching. Version control also provides evidence of process for a project portfolio, which is a marked criterion in the SEP.

questions.stem: The difference between a local and a remote repository is that a remote repo:
options: Runs the deployed application, while the local repo holds only the source code
Holds only the latest version, while the local repo holds the full commit history
Cannot hold branches — branches exist only locally until they are merged
Sits on a hosting service such as GitHub, enabling collaboration and backup, synchronised by push and pull
questions.explanation: (B) is the most commonly chosen wrong answer: Git is distributed, so a local clone holds the complete history, which is why you can commit and view the log with no network connection at all.

questions.stem: Open-source software's most cited security argument is:
options: Open-source licences oblige maintainers to patch reported vulnerabilities within a defined period
Because the source is published and auditable, open-source software has measurably fewer vulnerabilities than proprietary software
Community review means many eyes may examine the code, though maintenance is variable and support is not guaranteed
Publishing the source gives attackers no advantage, since they would find the same flaws by testing anyway
questions.explanation: (B) overclaims what the argument actually supports — Heartbleed and Log4Shell both sat in extremely widely used open-source code for years. A balanced answer also names licence obligations that may require you to open your own code, and links to "vulnerable and outdated components".

questions.stem: A CMS such as WordPress offers which trade-off?
options: A reduced attack surface, since the platform's core code is centrally maintained and patched
Complete control over the stack, at the cost of a much slower initial build
Fast deployment and easy content management for non-technical users, at the cost of less granular control
No hosting requirement, since the platform serves the site from its own infrastructure
questions.explanation: (A) is the inviting trap and is close to backwards: WordPress powers roughly 43% of websites, and its plugin ecosystem is one of the most-cited sources of vulnerable-component risk precisely because it is so widely deployed.

questions.stem: Lazy loading reduces initial page load time by:
options: Compressing images to a smaller file size before they are uploaded
Delaying the download of off-screen images until the user scrolls near them
Caching the whole page so that a repeat visit loads from disk
Loading a low-resolution placeholder first and swapping in the full image once it arrives
questions.explanation: Implemented with loading="lazy" on <img> tags. (D) is progressive loading — a different technique that still downloads the whole image, just in a more useful order. The mechanism — the initial load fetches only what is visible — is where the mark is.

questions.stem: A CDN reduces load time because:
options: It compresses HTML, CSS and JavaScript before transmission, cutting bandwidth use
Cached static content is served from servers physically closer to the user, cutting latency
It removes the need for the origin server to run a database at all
It combines many small requests into a single request, reducing the number of round trips
questions.explanation: Latency is largely a function of physical distance and round trips; bandwidth is how much can flow per second. (A) is compression and (D) is HTTP/2 multiplexing — both genuine optimisations, neither is what a CDN does.

questions.stem: Minification improves performance by:
options: Stripping whitespace and comments and shortening internal names in CSS/JS to reduce file size
Re-encoding images at lower quality so they download faster
Splitting a large bundle into smaller files that are loaded only when needed
Removing CSS rules that no selector anywhere on the site matches
questions.explanation: Tools: UglifyJS, CSSNano. (C) is code splitting and (D) is PurgeCSS — three separate optimisations that are often run in the same build pipeline, which is what makes them adjacent.

questions.stem: Adding defer to a <script> tag:
options: Downloads the script in parallel with HTML parsing and executes it after parsing finishes, preserving source order
Prevents the script from executing until the user interacts with the page
Downloads the script in parallel and executes it the moment it arrives, regardless of order
Instructs the browser to cache the script permanently after the first load
questions.explanation: (C) is async — the sharpest possible near-miss, since both attributes avoid render-blocking and differ only in when they execute and whether order is preserved. Use defer when scripts depend on each other or on the DOM.

questions.stem: A question asking you to minimise page load times wants:
options: Ways to measure load time, such as the Network tab and a Lighthouse audit
A comparison of load times across different browsers and devices
Reasons load time matters, such as bounce rate and search ranking
Ways to reduce load time, such as compression, caching, a CDN and lazy loading
questions.explanation: 2025 marker feedback specifically penalised answers that described how to investigate load time when asked how to reduce it — which is exactly option (A). Read the verb before you read the topic.

questions.stem: The two files that make a website a PWA are:
options: A service worker script and a viewport meta tag
A web app manifest and a responsive stylesheet
A service worker script and a web app manifest
An offline cache manifest and a push-notification handler
questions.explanation: The service worker provides offline capability, background operation and push notifications; the manifest (a JSON file) enables home-screen installation with a name, icons, colours and launch behaviour. (D) names two plausible-sounding files, neither of which is the requirement.

questions.stem: A service worker is best described as:
options: A server-side process that handles incoming requests for the application
A background script, separate from the page, that intercepts network requests and serves cached responses
A JSON file describing the app's name, icons and launch behaviour
A browser thread that renders the page independently of the main thread
questions.explanation: The word "worker" makes (A) and (D) tempting — but it runs client-side and does not render anything. (C) is the manifest, its partner file. The browser can start a service worker on demand, which is what allows push notifications and background sync when the page is closed.

questions.stem: A PWA remains technically a website because:
options: It cannot be installed to the device's home screen
It has no ability to operate without a network connection
It cannot access device hardware such as the camera or GPS
It is delivered over the web and still runs inside a browser engine
questions.explanation: (A), (B) and (C) all name things a PWA can do — they are the gaps PWAs were designed to close. Its advantage is a single codebase with web distribution, plus installability, offline use, background operation, full-screen presentation and OS integration.

questions.stem: A platform-specific app is distinguished by:
options: Being developed with the vendor's SDK for one operating system and distributed through that vendor's app store
Being written in HTML, CSS and JavaScript but wrapped in a native shell for distribution
Being installable directly from the web without passing through an app store review
Running unchanged on any operating system that provides a compatible runtime
questions.explanation: (B) describes a hybrid app, a genuine third category that sits between native and PWA. Native benefits — icon access, offline and background operation, immersive UI, OS integration, store presence — are precisely the gaps a PWA closes.

questions.stem: Progressive enhancement means:
options: Providing a baseline of essential content and functionality to as many users as possible, with a richer experience where the browser supports it
Building for the newest browsers first and adding fallbacks only once users report problems
Loading a page's critical content first and deferring everything else until after the first paint
Releasing a minimal product and adding features in later versions
questions.explanation: (C) is the sharpest trap — that is critical rendering path optimisation, which is about speed, not about capability across devices. PWAs should feature-detect advanced APIs and provide fallbacks, e.g. telling the user a message could not be sent if Background Sync is unsupported.

questions.stem: The Background Sync API lets a PWA:
options: Receive messages pushed from the server while the page is closed
Keep the local cache in step with the server whenever the app is open
Upload the site's assets to a CDN in the background after deployment
Ask a service worker to retry a queued network request as soon as connectivity returns
questions.explanation: (A) is the Push API — a separate service worker capability from the same family. Background Sync is a textbook progressive-enhancement case: valuable where supported, gracefully degraded with a clear message where it is not.

questions.stem: Which set of measures best describes web accessibility?
options: Clear labels, forgiving error messages, consistent navigation and an undo option
Fast load times, small images and a layout that responds across breakpoints
Sufficient colour contrast, alt text, keyboard navigability, screen-reader compatibility and scalable text
HTTPS, a Content Security Policy and secure cookie attributes
questions.explanation: (A) is the trap — those are usability measures. The point that lifts an extended answer is that the two overlap: each accessibility measure framed as a minority accommodation also improves usability for everyone, since high contrast helps anyone reading in sunlight.

questions.stem: The standard to name when asked how you would make a web solution accessible is:
options: Section 508 of the US Rehabilitation Act
ATAG, from the W3C's Web Accessibility Initiative
AS/NZS ISO/IEC 27001
WCAG, from the W3C's Web Accessibility Initiative
questions.explanation: WCAG — content must be perceivable, operable, understandable and robust. (B) is a real WAI standard from the same family, but ATAG governs authoring tools (the software used to build content), not the content itself.

questions.stem: Usability and accessibility relate in that:
options: They trade off against each other, since accessible interfaces must be more verbose and explicit
Accessible design is generally a usability improvement for all users, not only a minority accommodation
Usability is a subset of accessibility, because an unusable interface is by definition inaccessible
They address separate audiences and are assessed against separate standards
questions.explanation: Usability covers learnability, efficiency, error prevention and recovery, and satisfaction — all of which accessible design supports. (C) has the containment relationship backwards and is the most sophisticated-sounding wrong answer here.

questions.stem: Semantic HTML elements such as <nav>, <main> and <header> matter because:
options: A page must use them to be indexed by search engines at all
The browser renders them measurably faster than generic <div> elements
They reduce the size of the document by removing the need for class attributes
They convey structural meaning to screen readers and other assistive technology
questions.explanation: A page of <div> soup is visually identical and structurally meaningless to a screen-reader user, who cannot then skip to the main content or navigate by landmark. (A) overstates a real but secondary SEO benefit.

questions.stem: Which clause filters individual rows in a SQL query?
options: HAVING
WHERE
GROUP BY
SELECT
questions.explanation: WHERE — (A) is the near-miss that is worth a mark on its own: HAVING also filters, but it filters groups after GROUP BY has aggregated them. SELECT chooses columns, FROM the table, ORDER BY sorts.

questions.stem: SELECT * FROM Customers WHERE Country = 'Spain' AND CustomerName LIKE 'G%'; returns customers:
options: In Spain, or whose name begins with G
In Spain and whose name ends with G
In Spain and whose name begins with G
In Spain and whose name contains G anywhere
questions.explanation: AND requires both conditions, which rules out (A). LIKE 'G%' anchors at the start — the % matches anything after the G. '%G' would be (B) and '%G%' would be (D).

questions.stem: To list products from most to least expensive you would write:
options: ORDER BY Price
ORDER BY Price ASC
ORDER BY Price DESC
GROUP BY Price DESC
questions.explanation: ORDER BY defaults to ascending, so (A) and (B) are the same statement written two ways and both give cheapest first. GROUP BY collapses rows rather than sorting them.

questions.stem: Which of these is an aggregate function?
options: UPPER()
COALESCE()
AVG()
ROUND()
questions.explanation: AVG() — All four are real SQL functions, but only AVG collapses many rows into one value. The aggregate set is MIN(), MAX(), COUNT(), SUM(), AVG() — typically used with GROUP BY.

questions.stem: SELECT subject, AVG(grade) FROM students GROUP BY subject; returns:
options: One row per subject, showing that subject's average grade
One row per student, showing their average grade across all subjects
A single row showing the average grade across every student
Every student's grade, sorted by subject
questions.explanation: GROUP BY collapses the rows into one per distinct value of the grouped column, and the aggregate is computed within each group. (C) is what you would get with no GROUP BY clause at all.

questions.stem: Joining three tables in a WHERE clause requires:
options: One join condition
Two join conditions connected by OR
Three join conditions connected by AND
Two join conditions connected by AND
questions.explanation: Joining n tables requires n − 1 join conditions, each linked with AND. (B) is the quiet killer — OR between join conditions produces a partial cross-product rather than a join, returning far too many rows.

questions.stem: SQL dot notation (Borrowers.Borrower_ID) is required when:
options: The column being referenced holds a string rather than a numeric value
More than one table is involved and a column name could belong to either of them
An aggregate function is used inside a GROUP BY query
A record is inserted into a table that has a foreign key
questions.explanation: It is also used with aliases and to reference database.table.column. The practical rule: once a query touches two tables, qualify every field name, not just the ambiguous ones.

questions.stem: The most common SQL mistake penalised in the 2025 paper was:
options: Writing SQL keywords in lowercase rather than uppercase
Omitting quotation marks around string values in a WHERE clause
Using SELECT * instead of naming the required columns
Placing ORDER BY before WHERE in the statement
questions.explanation: WHERE Country = Spain fails; WHERE Country = 'Spain' works. Numbers are unquoted; strings and dates are quoted. (A) is a style preference and (C) is a habit, not an error — only (D) is also a genuine fault, but a far rarer one.

questions.stem: Which statement modifies the data in existing rows?
options: SELECT ... INTO
INSERT INTO ... VALUES
ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN
UPDATE ... SET ... WHERE
questions.explanation: UPDATE — (C) is the near-miss: ALTER TABLE modifies the table's structure, not the data in its rows. Always include a WHERE clause — UPDATE students SET grade = 95 with no WHERE rewrites every row in the table.

questions.stem: SQL is described as a declarative language because:
options: Every table and column must be declared in a schema before any data can be inserted
Statements execute strictly in the order written, one line at a time, as in a procedural script
Every variable used in a query must be declared with its type before the query runs
You state what result you want, and the database's query planner decides how to obtain it
questions.explanation: (A) is the trap that catches careful students: it is a true statement about SQL, and it contains the word "declared" — but it describes schema definition, not the declarative paradigm. The query planner deciding execution strategy is why the same result can be retrieved by very different physical plans.

questions.stem: A PWA stores learner-driver journal entries offline and syncs them when the device reconnects. The component that intercepts requests and serves cached content while offline is:
options: The service worker
The web app manifest
The viewport meta tag
The browser's local storage API
questions.explanation: Service worker — it sits between the page and the network, serving cached responses when the network is unavailable, and can use Background Sync to send queued entries on reconnection. (D) is the tempting one: local storage holds the data, but it cannot intercept a request or act while the page is closed.

questions.stem: A comment field on a PWA renders user-submitted HTML directly into the DOM. The vulnerability and its fix are:
options: Cross-site scripting; sanitise with a library such as DOMPurify before insertion, plus output encoding and a CSP
Cross-site request forgery; add a per-session token to the comment form and set SameSite cookies
SQL injection; replace string concatenation with parameterised queries
Insecure design; move comment rendering to the server so user content never reaches the DOM
questions.explanation: (D) sounds architecturally sophisticated but is wrong on both halves — server-rendered HTML is just as vulnerable if it is not sanitised, and the flaw is a specific, well-named one rather than a design category. Verification method worth naming: submit a <script> tag and confirm it is stored and rendered as inert text.

questions.stem: A site takes 9 seconds to load on mobile. Which set of changes most directly addresses this?
options: Rewrite the back end in a compiled language and add a database connection pool
Add server RAM and CPU, and move the database onto faster storage
Compress and lazy-load images, minify and split JavaScript, serve static assets from a CDN, enable caching, and defer non-critical scripts
Add a loading spinner and skeleton screens so the wait feels shorter to the user
questions.explanation: (A) and (B) attack server processing time, which is rarely the bottleneck on mobile — network transfer is. (D) improves perceived performance without changing the measurement. Give the mechanism for each change: fewer bytes over the network, shorter physical distance, no re-download, no render blocking. The mechanism is the mark.

questions.stem: A developer stores a session token in localStorage. The main security concern is:
options: It is transmitted with every request, so it appears in server access logs
It is readable by any other site the user visits in the same browser
It is cleared when the tab is closed, so the user is logged out unexpectedly
It persists with no expiry and is readable by any JavaScript running on the page, so an XSS flaw exposes it
questions.explanation: (A) describes cookies, (C) describes session storage, and (B) is false — local storage is scoped by origin. An HttpOnly cookie is not reachable from JavaScript at all, which is why session identifiers generally belong there, with Secure and SameSite also set.

questions.stem: Choosing NoSQL over SQL is best justified when:
options: Records have varying fields, the schema evolves quickly, and horizontal scaling matters more than complex joins
Strong referential integrity across many related tables is the primary requirement
The workload is dominated by multi-table joins and aggregate reporting queries
The dataset is small enough to sit comfortably in memory on a single server
questions.explanation: (B) and (C) are the two cases that argue for SQL. Justify by matching the data shape and access pattern to the model, and say explicitly why the alternative is worse for this case rather than in general.

questions.stem: A front-end and a back-end team disagree about a response format mid-project. The preventive practice is:
options: Having the back-end team publish the database schema so the front end can mirror its field names
Agreeing the data contract — the shape of the data the API sends and receives — before either side builds against it
Having the front-end team build only against live back-end endpoints, from the first sprint onward
Deferring the format decision until integration, when both sides understand their real needs
questions.explanation: An agreed contract lets both sides work in parallel against a stub. (D) is the actual failure mode dressed up as a plan, and (A) leaks the internal schema into the public API — a design smell in its own right.

questions.stem: Shell scripting contributes to a web workflow by:
options: Automating repeatable sequences — building, testing, deploying, moving files and running backups
Generating the HTML that the web server returns for each incoming request
Managing which version of each dependency the project installs
Monitoring the running application and alerting when a threshold is crossed
questions.explanation: It is the manual ancestor of a CI/CD pipeline — the same steps, run by hand rather than automatically on every commit. (C) is a package manager and (D) is a monitoring tool; both are commonly invoked from shell scripts, which is why they feel close.

questions.stem: A site works in Chrome but breaks in Safari. The most likely cause and remedy are:
options: An expired TLS certificate; renew it and redeploy
Rendering-engine differences in feature support; test cross-browser and use feature detection with fallbacks
A missing viewport meta tag; add it so the layout scales on the device
A CORS policy that Safari enforces and Chrome does not; widen the list of allowed origins
questions.explanation: (D) is the most sophisticated distractor and is wrong on the premise — both browsers enforce CORS, and "widen the allowed origins" would be a security regression rather than a fix. Browsers implement standards at different times, which is exactly why progressive enhancement and feature detection exist.

questions.stem: An SSL/TLS certificate contains all of the following except:
options: The domain name it was issued for
The issuing CA's digital signature
The server's public key
The server's private key
questions.explanation: The private key never leaves the server — if it were in the certificate, which is served to every visitor, the entire scheme would collapse. The certificate also carries an expiry date; an expired certificate produces the browser warning users are trained to click through.

questions.stem: For a page that must work on a slow rural connection, the highest-value single change is usually:
options: Adding a service worker so that repeat visits load from cache
Serving assets from a CDN with edge locations closer to the user
Enabling HTTP/2 so many resources share a single connection
Reducing the total bytes transferred — compressing images and removing unused CSS and JavaScript
questions.explanation: All four are genuine optimisations — the discriminator is which constraint binds. On a bandwidth-limited link, payload size dominates; (B) and (C) attack latency, and (A) does nothing at all for the visit that matters most, the first one. On a high-bandwidth but distant link the answer would be (B) — match the fix to the constraint.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest justification for an external stylesheet over inline styles on a 40-page site?
options: External stylesheets parse faster, because the browser can process them in parallel with the HTML
Inline styles are invalid HTML and will fail validation
One change propagates to every page, the file is cached once across the whole site, and the markup stays readable
The browser ignores inline styles whenever a linked stylesheet is also present
questions.explanation: Maintainability is the argument, and the caching benefit compounds across 40 pages. (D) is the reverse of the truth — inline styles beat everything short of !important, which is exactly what makes them so painful to override later.

questions.stem: A page uses only colour to indicate which form fields are invalid. The accessibility failure is:
options: The error state is not announced until the whole form is submitted
The contrast ratio between the error colour and the background is likely below 4.5:1
Meaning is conveyed by colour alone, which excludes colour-blind users and screen-reader users
The error colour cannot be overridden by the user's operating system theme
questions.explanation: (A) and (B) are both real WCAG concerns — contrast and timely feedback — but they are different criteria, and each might be satisfied while this failure persists. The fix: add a text message, an icon, and a programmatic association between the error and the field so assistive technology announces it.

questions.stem: Which best explains why HTTPS matters for a PWA specifically?
options: Cached responses are written to disk in encrypted form only when they arrived over HTTPS
The web app manifest can only be served over HTTPS, so the app cannot otherwise be installed
WCAG requires a secure connection for any installable web application
Service workers require a secure context, because a worker able to intercept every request would be catastrophic over an interceptable connection
questions.explanation: The reasoning is the mark: a service worker is designed to sit in front of the network, so an attacker who could inject one over plain HTTP would own every subsequent request permanently. Powerful browser APIs are gated behind HTTPS for exactly this reason.

questions.stem: An INSERT succeeds, but the record cannot be found by a later SELECT ... WHERE name = Amelia. The most likely fault is:
options: The SELECT is querying a different table from the one the INSERT wrote to
The INSERT was never committed, so the new row is not yet visible to other queries
The string literal is unquoted — it should be 'Amelia'
String comparison in WHERE is case-sensitive, so the stored value does not match
questions.explanation: Unquoted text is parsed as a column name, not a value — so the query either errors or compares the column to itself. (B) and (D) are real failure modes in other situations, which is what makes them plausible here.

questions.stem: Which combination correctly matches protocol to purpose?
options: IMAP sends mail · SMTP keeps mail synchronised on the server · DNS resolves names to IP addresses
SMTP sends mail · POP3 keeps mail synchronised on the server · DNS resolves names to IP addresses
SMTP sends mail · IMAP keeps mail synchronised on the server · DHCP resolves names to IP addresses
SMTP sends mail · IMAP keeps mail synchronised on the server · DNS resolves names to IP addresses
questions.explanation: Each distractor swaps exactly one element, so all three look right at a glance. SMTP 25 send-only · IMAP 143 sync and keep · POP3 110 download and remove · DNS 53 name resolution · DHCP assigns addresses.

questions.stem: A team wants to add a feature without destabilising the live site. The correct version-control practice is:
options: Commit directly to main but tag the last known-good commit so it can be restored if needed
Create a branch, develop and test in isolation, then merge back after review
Clone the repository into a second folder, develop there, and copy the files back when finished
Develop on main behind a feature flag, so the code ships but stays switched off
questions.explanation: (D) is a genuine industry technique, but it is a deployment strategy layered on top of version control rather than an answer to this question — and used alone it puts untested code on main. (C) is what version control exists to replace. Small, frequent commits and short-lived branches also minimise the risk of a painful merge conflict.

questions.stem: A CMS-built site is repeatedly compromised through its plugins. The best structural response is:
options: Replace the CMS with a custom-built application so no third-party code is involved
Minimise the plugin footprint, keep everything patched, use only actively maintained plugins, and monitor
Restrict access to the admin panel to a small allowlist of IP addresses
Place the site behind a WAF tuned to block the CMS's known exploit signatures
questions.explanation: (C) and (D) are real, useful mitigations that leave the root cause untouched — the vulnerable code is still installed and still reachable through the public site. (A) trades a known problem for an unbounded one. This is the "vulnerable and outdated components" problem, and the CMS trade-off includes inheriting the security posture of every plugin you install.

questions.stem: In evaluating whether to build a PWA or a platform-specific app for a school project, the strongest justification structure is:
options: Describe the technical architecture of both options in equal detail, then state a preference
State the criteria (reach across devices, offline need, budget and team skills, distribution, OS feature access), assess both options against them, and conclude why the alternative is worse
List the features each option supports and choose whichever supports more of them
Identify the option most widely used for projects of this type and justify the choice by precedent
questions.explanation: All four are structures a student might use; only (B) is an evaluation. (C) is the seductive one — counting features looks rigorous but weights a rarely used capability the same as a decisive one. For a single-developer school project the PWA's single codebase and web distribution usually decide it, but say so explicitly rather than assuming it.

questions.stem: Which statement about caching is most accurate?
options: Caching trades freshness for speed, so the cache policy must match how often the resource actually changes
Caching always serves the newest version, because the browser revalidates a resource before every use
Caching should be applied uniformly to every resource, since the browser will revalidate anything that has changed
Caching removes the need for a CDN, since both simply store copies of the same content
questions.explanation: Static assets can be cached aggressively using versioned filenames; dynamic data cannot. (B) and (C) both assume revalidation the browser does not do unless the headers ask for it — which is exactly how users end up staring at a stale page. Browser caching uses Cache-Control/Expires; server-side caching uses Memcached or Redis.

questions.stem: A form posts a password over HTTP on a public Wi-Fi network. The specific attack this enables is:
options: Cross-site request forgery
Man-in-the-middle interception
Session fixation
A timing side-channel attack
questions.explanation: TLS defeats it twice over: encryption stops the eavesdropping, and the CA-issued certificate stops the impersonation half of the attack. The other three are real attacks that HTTPS alone does not prevent.

questions.stem: Which is the best evidence of veracity problems in a dataset feeding a web dashboard?
options: The dataset has grown beyond what a single server can process
Missing values, inconsistent formats, and records that contradict an independent source
New records arrive faster than the ingestion pipeline can consume them
The feed combines JSON, CSV and free-text fields in a single stream
questions.explanation: The distractors are the other three Vs: (A) volume, (C) velocity, (D) variety. Those describe the dataset's shape; veracity describes whether you can trust what it says.

questions.stem: In the request lifecycle, TLS negotiation occurs:
options: Before DNS resolution, so the certificate can be retrieved alongside the address
After the TCP handshake and before the HTTP request is sent
After the HTTP request is sent but before the response is returned
At the same time as packet reassembly on the destination device
questions.explanation: Resolve the name → open the connection (TCP) → secure the connection (TLS) → exchange HTTP → reassemble and render. TLS must come before the HTTP request, because the request itself — including its headers and any credentials — is what needs protecting.

questions.stem: A dev tools Console error reads Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read property 'value' of null. The most likely cause is:
options: The script ran before the element existed in the DOM — load it with defer or attach on DOMContentLoaded
The element exists but its value property is empty, which JavaScript reports as null
The selector matched more than one element, so the lookup returned null rather than choosing between them
The CSS file failed to load, so the element was never rendered onto the page
questions.explanation: null means the element lookup itself found nothing — a timing or selector problem, not a network one. (B) and (C) are both plausible-sounding misconceptions: an empty value is "", and a multi-match returns the first element, not null.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly distinguishes bandwidth from latency?
options: Bandwidth is the theoretical maximum rate; latency is the rate actually achieved in practice
Bandwidth is the delay before transfer begins; latency is how much data can flow per unit time
Bandwidth is measured end-to-end; latency is measured only at the server
Bandwidth is how much data can flow per unit time; latency is the delay before transfer begins
questions.explanation: (A) is the subtle one — it describes bandwidth versus throughput, both of which are rates. Latency is a time, not a rate. Compression and minification address bandwidth; CDNs, caching, fewer requests and HTTP/2-3 multiplexing address latency.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest concluding judgement in an 8-mark question on a web solution?
options: "The PWA approach was chosen because a single codebase reaches every device, which matters more for a solo developer than the deeper OS integration a native app would have offered."
"The solution uses a service worker for offline access, a manifest for installation, lazy loading and a CDN for performance, and semantic HTML with WCAG AA contrast for accessibility."

"Judged against load performance, accessibility and offline reliability, the PWA meets its purpose — sub-two-second first load through lazy loading and a CDN, WCAG AA contrast and full keyboard operation, and offline journal entry via the service worker — though push notifications remain unsupported on some browsers, so the design feature-detects and degrades gracefully."
"Compared with a platform-specific app, the PWA loads faster on first use but has narrower access to device hardware, and is distributed over the web rather than through an app store."
questions.explanation: Criteria named, evidence given against each, limitation acknowledged with its mitigation, judgement made — and tied to this solution rather than to PWAs in general. The others are each a different directive verb executed well: (B) describes, (A) justifies, (D) compares.
